chapter_theme: Songs at Vaitheeswaran Koyil (வைத்தீசுரன் கோயில், the Velur of the physician Lord): the poet confesses the darkness of mala, countless births in delusion and the lure of courtesans, and asks for the feet of wisdom, the company of devotees and the yogic ascent to nectar; the praise names Murugan as lord of the healer's shrine.
structure_note: Short plea against mala (779); births and maya (780, 782); courtesans (781, 784); and a full kundalini song (783) that sets the body's yoga against the courtesan's bed of the next.

779.reading: The poet says he cannot speak even a little of Murugan, the unique wisdom of the heart, and asks whether, like a block of wood, he should perish covered in the darkness of mala. The praise names Murugan the life of those of high virtue, who grants life at his feet, son of the just giver of boons, Vaidyanatha the lord.
779.nuance: மரத்துறை போல், like a thing of wood, is the image of the unaware soul, and மலத்திருள் the darkness of impurity of Siddhanta. வயித்திய நாதப் பெருமாளே: the shrine's name for Siva, the physician, is given to Murugan.

780.reading: The poet asks how many crores of bodies he has left after running and dancing in them, how many have gone, how often he has fallen into such pleasure and what will come hereafter; caught in the tangle of mean maya, which on thought is only 'chi, chi', he asks for the wondrous feet of wisdom sung by the masters of the three Tamils. The praise shows Murugan dancing in the hearts of those who chant him daily as his house, son of the formless Siva who is half green and bears the trident, on the peacock that tears the thousand-headed serpent, at Velur of the areca and the leaping fish.
780.nuance: எத்தனை கோடி கோடி விட்டுடல்: the count of bodies left behind opens the song, as in 493. சீசீ, the cry of disgust, is set inside the plea. நிட்கள ரூபர் பாதி பச்சுரு: Siva the partless with the green half that is Uma.

781.reading: The poet describes women with anklets and silk, like painted dolls, breasts like tower peaks and speech like cane and sugar, who walk the streets with bees around their hair singing like flocks of birds, flatter and trick, saying 'bring money first, then what you like', and set up a ladder for a man to climb, and asks whether this is to be his lot. The praise shows the demons destroyed, hills and seas dried by the vel, gods raining flowers, sages as heralds and Lakshmi praising, Murugan singing to Valli in the millet field, and the child who comes dancing to give kisses at the praise of Siva of the hill of wisdom and his consort.
781.nuance: வாரும் முற்பணம் தாரும் இட்டமென, 'come, give the money first, then as you please', is the courtesans' own speech. ஏணி வைத்து வந்து ஏற விட்டிடுவர் may mean they lift a man up only to drop him; the image is not clear. நாதர் மெச்ச வந்து ஆடு முத்தம் அருள்: Murugan as the child giving kisses to his parents.

782.reading: The poet calls himself a belly raised on rags and rice, a mind that takes changing forms, wasted by unjust maya, and asks Murugan to pity him so that he is not born and does not die again: to burn the hosts of deeds to dust with the vel, set him among the devotees who keep his house of release, make his mind like Murugan's own, and let him say 'Kanda Vel is mine'. The praise names the vel that killed the Suras spread like wind, Siva of the bull as father, Valli embraced, and Murugan who dwells in the love of devotees, worshipped by gods, siddhas and servants at Velur with the cock banner.
782.nuance: The plea climbs from release from birth to burning deeds (வினைக்கணங்கள் தூளதா எரித்து), to the company of devotees (அன்பர்கண் மேவி), to likeness of mind (உனைப்போல் சிந்தையாக). The line on Siva who burnt Kama's arrows and 'embraced endless crores of women' (காம பாணம் அட்ட நந்த கோடி மாதரைப் புணர்ந்த) is obscure.

783.reading: The poet describes the yogic ascent: raising the fire from the root centre through the six supports, driving the breath up the middle channel, hearing the music of nada, the milk-white light and the self held fast, then mounting the seat of mantra in the city of wisdom where mother and father sit, and asks Murugan to show him the three lights in that house, feed him the honeyed nectar of the moon and rule him. The praise names Uma who bears the trident and guards day and night, Siva who cured disease and deed at Velur, and Murugan's vel that dried the seven seas, the peacock and his pity for Vishnu's daughter.
783.nuance: The plea is technical yoga: மூலாதாரம், ஆறாதாரம், சுழிமுனை, நாதம், and the moon's nectar (சந்திர ... தேனமுது). வீடே மூணொளி காட்டி: in the house of release, show the three lights (perhaps sun, moon and fire). சூடோடு ஈர்வினை வாட்டி ... வாழ்வினை தீர்த்த சங்கரர்: the healing at Vaitheeswaran is named in passing. Several syllable runs in the first half are hard to divide.

784.reading: The poet describes women with swaying hair, breasts, earrings and eyes, scent rising from them, gait like a peacock, anklets ringing and voices like cuckoos, who gather in the streets, call passers-by 'come', melt with play, take them home and embrace them, and asks whether, having sunk in their breasts and sweated on the bed, he must wander in a sea of colic and many diseases. The praise gathers the serpent world, moon and sun worlds, Brahma's world, the gods, ganas, Siva, Brahmins and sages, Narayana, Puranas and Vedic song around the vel thrown at the hill, Valli embraced, and Murugan at Velur on the Kaveri.
784.nuance: வீதிவருவோரை வாருமெனவே, calling passers-by in the street, and மனையே கொடு அணைவார்கள், taking them home, mark the courtesans. The end of the confession is disease (சூலை பல நோய்கள் கடலாடி), the cost of the bed. The song ends with Velur, but the Kaveri lies some way off.

links.note: Tirumular's bindu in the root centre is raised by fire past the throat and becomes cool nectar at the moon; 783 asks Murugan for the same path, root fire through the six supports to the moon's honeyed nectar, as a gift of grace rather than a discipline.

source_issues: Songs 780, 783, 784: one corrupt character each in §வ்ளுர் (lines 15, 17 and 24), for வேளூர், the shrine's name.
Song 783: முலாதாரமொ (line 1) is probably மூலாதாரமொ, an unflagged loss of the long vowel.
The chapter heading names Vaitheeswaran Koyil; the songs call it வேளூர் (Pullirukkuvelur).
